"Remember the hostel terrace?" Pema said, stirring her coffee. "Instant noodles at midnight, singing badly. Best years of our lives."
Ira smiled. "They were lovely. I still make noodles when work gets heavy, just to feel that again."
"And now look at us. Rent, bosses, bills. It's all downhill."
"Is it, though? Pema, you cried every week about money back then."
"I did, didn't I."
"And I was so lonely that first year I nearly dropped out," Ira said. "I forget that too, when I get nostalgic, so I make myself remember it."
"So it wasn't great?"
"It was great and hard. The terrace taught me to make friends from nothing. I use that every day at the new office."
Pema laughed. "Fine. Terrace skills, applied."
"Exactly. I'll bring the noodles on Saturday," she said.

qa.q: What does Ira still make when work gets heavy?
qa.a: Noodles, just to feel that hostel feeling again.

qa.q: Why does Ira bring up her lonely first year?
qa.a: She enjoys the memory but wants an honest picture, so she makes herself remember that the hostel years were hard too.

qa.q: What does Ira carry from the past into her present?
qa.a: The skill of making friends from nothing, which she uses at the new office, so the memory adds to now instead of making it look poor.

qa.q: How does Pema's view shift during the talk?
qa.a: Pema starts by calling life all downhill, then remembers her own money worries and laughs about applying terrace skills now.

grounding: A young woman enjoys hostel memories as comfort and a source of skills while deliberately recalling the loneliness, so the present keeps its value.

passage:
Last month I went back to Siliguri for the first time in six years, and I was sure I'd return to Pune miserable.
I walked past our old rented house, the tea stall, the school gate. My chest ached in the best way. Baba used to buy me, his only daughter, hot jalebis at that stall. Arnab, my brother, and I would race home in the rain.
On the train back, I caught myself thinking: life was so much sweeter then. So I made myself finish the thought honestly. The roof leaked every monsoon. Baba lost his job the year I was nine, and I remember the silence at dinner.
Both are true. The sweetness taught me to make small treats matter, which I still do. The hard parts remind me that my small flat in Pune, with its steady roof, is not nothing.
That's how I keep the old days now: as a warm shawl, not a measuring stick.
Kalyani

qa.q: Which town did Kalyani visit for the first time in six years?
qa.a: Siliguri.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling as she walked past the old house and tea stall?
qa.a: Her chest ached in the best way: a warm, sweet longing for the childhood with Baba and Arnab. 🤍

qa.q: How does Kalyani stop the trip from making Pune feel poor?
qa.a: She finishes the thought honestly, recalling the leaking roof and Baba's lost job, and keeps the lesson of small treats, so the past is comfort, not a measuring stick.

qa.q: How might Arnab remember the same childhood?
qa.a: Arnab might also treasure racing home in the rain, and could carry his own memories of the leaks and the quiet dinners that year.

grounding: A young woman revisits her childhood town, savours the warmth, then honestly recalls the hardships so her present life does not seem poor.

passage:
Mentoring notes, Maria, programme coordinator

Tanuja came back from her college reunion glowing. In our check-in she showed me photos: the old canteen, the debate trophy, her classmates in matching kurtas. "I felt twenty again," she said.

Then she added something I wrote down. "On the bus I started thinking our college team was better than my team here. So I made a list of what was hard then too: the exam panic, the hostel curfew, the friend I fell out with. That helped."

She said she wants to bring the reunion spirit into work, not measure work against it. Her idea: a short Friday story circle where volunteers share one good memory and one lesson.

What I did next: approved a trial of three Fridays, and asked her to lead the first.

qa.q: What idea did Tanuja bring back from the reunion?
qa.a: A short Friday story circle where volunteers share one good memory and one lesson.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja make a list on the bus?
qa.a: Tanuja felt uneasy when she caught herself thinking the college team was better than her team now, so she made the list to get an honest picture and keep the past from spoiling the present.

qa.q: What makes Tanuja's approach a healthy use of nostalgia?
qa.a: She enjoys the reunion glow and turns it into something useful at work, while the list of hard things stops unfair comparisons.

qa.q: How does Maria respond to Tanuja's glow?
qa.a: Maria takes it seriously, writes down her words, approves a three-Friday trial and trusts Tanuja to lead the first.

grounding: A coordinator records how a young woman enjoys reunion memories, lists what was hard back then, and brings the good spirit into her current work.

passage:
Sunday night
Zubin dug out my old school autograph book today while clearing the loft. I sat on the floor for an hour, smiling like a fool. "Friends forever," "Don't forget me, Ritu," little hearts in gel pen. The winter we all shared one blanket on the school trip to Shimla. God, I miss that.
Then I made myself remember the rest: maths tuition that made my stomach hurt, our one-room flat with one fan fighting over it, Papa's worried face at the end of every month. It was not a golden time. It was a good-and-hard time.
Zubin teased, "Madam is time-travelling again." Fine, I am. But what I really want to keep from those years is how we shared. Our little flat now isn't poor compared to that; it just needs more people in it. Inviting the Shimla gang for Diwali. 🙂

qa.q: What did Zubin find while clearing the loft?
qa.a: Ritu's old school autograph book.

qa.q: Why did Ritu make herself remember the maths tuition and the one-fan flat?
qa.a: She enjoyed the warm memories but didn't want them to turn into a fake golden past that made her present life seem poorer.

qa.q: What did Ritu decide to carry forward from the old days, and what step did she plan?
qa.a: The habit of sharing; she plans to invite the Shimla gang for Diwali.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Ritu's hour on the floor with the autograph book?
qa.a: Zubin seems fond and amused, teasing Ritu about time-travelling while letting her enjoy it.

grounding: A diary shows a young woman enjoying nostalgia and drawing values from it, while reminding herself of what was hard then.

passage: Sarika walked with her cousin Baljeet along the canal road outside their village near Moga, past the old peepal where they used to hide in summer. "Remember the mangoes from Tayaji's orchard? The whole gang, barefoot?" Baljeet grinned. "And now children just sit on phones." Sarika laughed, then stopped herself. She remembered the other things too: the walk to the one-room school through ankle-deep mud, the roof that leaked on their slates, the winter her friend Gurmeet left school for good. "The mangoes were the best part," she said. "The mud was not." Now she taught in the new school at the crossing, and the children came on a bus. She still kept one thing from those summers: on the last day of term she took her class to the orchard, barefoot if they liked.

qa.q: Where did Sarika now teach?
qa.a: In the new school at the crossing.

qa.q: Why does Sarika stop herself after laughing at Baljeet's comment?
qa.a: She feels fond of the memories but also uneasy with the complaint, because she remembers the mud, the leaking roof and her friend leaving school, and does not want the past to make today look poor.

passage: Sunday afternoon in Durban, and Dalia had the old playlist from her student days on while she cooked. "This song," she told her flatmate Zanele, swaying. "Third year, the flat on Umbilo Road. We'd make a giant pot of soup and whoever was broke that week ate free." Zanele smiled. "Sounds like heaven." Dalia stirred and thought about it. The flat had also had a broken geyser for five months. She'd cried in the bathroom before every exam. She had once been so lonely she spoke to nobody for a whole weekend. "It was heaven sometimes," she said. "Mostly it was the soup." She looked at the pot. "Actually, why don't we do that here? Sunday soup, anyone from the building can come." Zanele was already writing the note for the lift.

qa.q: What did Dalia and her friends cook in the Umbilo Road flat?
qa.a: They made a giant pot of soup.

qa.q: What is Dalia feeling as she stirs the pot and remembers the old flat?
qa.a: She feels warm and nostalgic about the soup nights but also a little sad, remembering the broken geyser, the exam tears and the lonely weekend.

qa.q: Which choice turns Dalia's nostalgia into something useful?
qa.a: She keeps the value from the past, sharing soup with whoever needs it, and brings it into her present life instead of just mourning the old flat.

qa.q: How might Zanele experience the new Sunday soup plan?
qa.a: Zanele seems excited and included, since Dalia's memory turns into something they can share now rather than a story she can only listen to.

grounding: Shows a young adult enjoying nostalgia for student life while honestly recalling its hardships and carrying its best value into the present.

passage: In the staff room of the Jaipur school, the talk turned to college. Vinita, who taught maths, sighed. "Those were the golden years. No parents' meetings, no marking." Kiran, twenty-six and three years into teaching English, felt the pull too: hostel terrace, late-night songs, everyone sharing tiffins. She let herself enjoy it for a moment. Then she remembered the rest: the night before finals when she couldn't breathe for worry, the roommate who stopped speaking to her, her father's illness in second year. "Golden, and also terrifying," she said. Vinita laughed. "True. I failed stats once." Kiran opened her tiffin and pushed it into the middle of the table. "The sharing part we can still do." Vinita added her aloo parathas. The bell rang, and neither of them rushed.

qa.q: What subject did Vinita teach?
qa.a: Vinita taught maths.

qa.q: Why did Kiran let herself enjoy the college memory before remembering the hard parts?
qa.a: She felt warm and comforted by the hostel memories, and enjoying them felt safe because she also knew to recall the worry, the roommate and her father's illness.

qa.q: What small step did Kiran take to carry the best of the past into the present?
qa.a: She pushed her tiffin into the middle of the table so the staff could share, keeping the value of college days without mourning them.

qa.q: How does Vinita's view of college change during the conversation?
qa.a: Vinita starts by calling college the golden years, but after Kiran's honest reply she admits failing stats and joins in sharing food.

Dear Vijay,

You asked if I still miss college. I do. Last week I found our hostel photos: the terrace chai at midnight, the fest where we painted the whole corridor. I sat on the floor smiling for an hour.

But I also made myself remember the rest. The exam panics. The fights about the bathroom roster. How lonely the first semester was.

It's funny. The warm memories remind me what I care about: friends, late talks, trying new things. So now I'm trying to find that here. I've joined a Sunday painting group in the city. It's not the hostel terrace, but it's mine.

Hope your new job is kind to you.

Jahnavi

qa.a: A Sunday painting group in the city.

qa.a: Jahnavi feels warm and nostalgic, smiling for an hour, while also remembering the hard parts.

I'm Parul, and you want to know if I miss my village? Of course. The smell of rain on the mud courtyard, my Ganga mausi's songs at night, the mango season. When I first moved to Delhi, I'd sit on my tiny balcony and feel like my life had become grey.

Then one day I remembered other things too. The long walk for water. The school with one teacher for four classes. How much Ma worried when the crops failed.

I still love those memories. They remind me what matters: family, music, being outdoors. So now I call Ganga mausi every Sunday, and I sing with her on the phone. I grow chillies in pots on that tiny balcony.

The past is sweet. But I don't let it make now look poor.

qa.q: What does Parul grow on the balcony?
qa.a: Chillies in pots.

qa.q: How did Parul feel at first after moving to Delhi?
qa.a: Parul felt homesick and low, as if life had become grey compared with the village.

qa.q: What did Parul do with the values the memories held?
qa.a: Parul began calling Ganga mausi every Sunday to sing together and grew chillies on the balcony, bringing family, music and green things into the present.

I've shared a flat with Charu for a year, and I've noticed how she handles missing home.

Some evenings she puts on old film songs her father loved and makes her mother's rajma. She gets a faraway look. Once, our friend Dilnaz said, "You make it sound like your hometown was heaven."

Charu laughed. "It wasn't. The power went off every evening. The buses were awful. Papa and I fought all the time about my studies."

Then she added, "But the rajma is still the best."

I can't tell exactly what she feels on those evenings. She doesn't seem sad for long. The next day she's back at work, planning a weekend trip, making new plans in this city.

passage: Vijay, you keep saying school was better than your new job. Let me tell you about your Nandini nani at twenty-five. I had just moved to the city after my wedding, and I missed my village so much I made everyone around me miserable. "In the village the mangoes were sweeter, the people kinder," I'd say. One evening my mother-in-law asked, "Were they kinder when the well dried up and you walked two hours for water?" I was angry. But that night I wrote two lines in my diary: what I loved, and what was hard. Every year after, I read both. I still cook village food on Sundays, beta. But I stopped telling your nana the city was poor. It was only new.

passage: Pallavi's train home for Diwali was cancelled at the last minute, and every other train was full. So she spent the evening alone in her rented room in Hyderabad, the neighbours' crackers booming. She let herself remember Diwali at home: rangoli with her mother, laddoos, cousins everywhere. Then, gently, she reminded herself of the rest: the cousins' fights, the aunties asking when she would marry, the year the power failed and nobody slept. The warmth was real, and so was the noise. She lit two diyas on her window ledge. When her friend Farida knocked with a box of kaju katli from her office, Pallavi laughed. "Now it's a festival," she said, making room on the floor.

qa.a: Her train home was cancelled at the last minute, and every other train was full.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have felt while the neighbours' crackers boomed?

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that stopped the past making the present feel poor?

An old radio song came on while Bidisha and Naveen were folding laundry in their Kolkata flat, and she stopped, a shirt in her hands. "This played in Baba's shop every evening. The whole lane would stop to listen. Life was so simple then."
Naveen smiled. "You miss it."
"I do." She hummed along. Then she added, more slowly, "Simple, and also hard. Baba worked fourteen hours a day. We shared one bathroom with three families. Ma worried about money every month."
She hung the shirt up. "I want to keep what that lane taught me, everyone stopping for each other. But I don't want to pretend our life now is poor just because it's busier."
Naveen turned the volume up, and they finished the laundry singing, badly.

qa.q: Where did the song play every evening in Bidisha's memory?
qa.a: In Baba's shop.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel when the song comes on?

qa.q: What makes Bidisha's way of remembering healthy?
